newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai breastfeeding low, unethical practices blamed.
newsitem.headline: Thai breastfeeding low, unethical practices blamed.

text.p: Thailand has the lowest level of breastfeeding mothers in Asia and among the lowest in the world, due partly to unethical marketing practices by infant formula manufacturers, UNICEF said on Wednesday.
Only about four percent of Thai mothers exclusively breastfeed their infants, the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) said in its Progress of Nations 1997 report.

"Despite undisputed evidence that exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months ensures infants' proper nutrition and safeguards their overall health, multinationals...are distributing literature promoting infant formula over breast milk and giving away formula to mothers," said the report, obtained by Reuters on Wednesday.

It said the practices were violations of the International Code of Marketing of Breastmilk Substitutes adopted in 1981 to protect breastfeeding and to strictly regulate the marketing of breast-milk substitutes.

"Recent studies indicate that just four percent of Thai mothers are exclusively breastfeeding their infants, while 44 percent of infants in the developing world are exclusively breastfed," the report said.
Countries with the highest rate of breastfeeding mothers include Rwanda and Burundi, where nearly 90 percent of mothers breastfeed.
UNICEF and the World Health Organisation recommended that babies be fed only breastmilk for about the first six months of life.
Studies show that babies who are fed infant formula instead of being exclusively breastfed have 10 times the risk of incurring bacterial infections requiring hospitalisation.
They also are four times more at risk of contracting meningitis and have three to four times the risk of developing middle ear infections and gastroenteritis.
The report said the reduction of infant formula use and improved breastfeeding practices world-wide could save the lives of an estimated 1.5 million children per year.
The small percentage of breastfeeding mothers in Thailand could be partly due to an increasing number of women working outside the home, the study said.
But it said the numbers were more likely due to intense marketing by infant formula manufacturers.

It quoted a study in Thailand in late 1996 that showed that 25 percent of mothers surveyed reported receiving either literature promoting benefits of formula over breastmilk or free samples of formula.

"Free samples, especially those handed out by health professionals, are a particularly insidious form of promotion," the report said. "A mother can easily switch from breast to bottle, but from bottle to breast is another story."
